summary: The note surveys how governments in the post-COVID era manage foreign direct investment and exchange rates, noting a shift toward tighter investment screening, more dynamic central bank currency tools, and a focus on sustainability and equity. It cites dated examples from Japan, Argentina, Canada and China, and describes the growing role of technology (AI, blockchain) and international coordination via the G20, WTO and IMF. It concludes that countries must balance openness with national interests while pursuing sustainable growth.
one_line: Overview of post-COVID trends in foreign investment controls and exchange rate management, including technology adoption, sustainability goals, and international coordination.
key_facts: After September 1, 2023, governments worldwide began reassessing foreign investment's role, balancing international capital against protecting local industries.

In late 2023 the United States and the European Union unveiled new regulatory frameworks to streamline foreign investments, focused on sectors crucial to national security and infrastructural resilience.

Dr. Emily Zhao of the London School of Economics argues that "The pendulum is swinging towards tighter controls on foreign direct investment (FDI)" while still recognizing the need for global cooperation.
On November 15, 2024, the Bank of Japan introduced a policy of targeted exchange rate corridors to maintain the yen's stability amid unpredictable capital flows.

On December 5, 2024, Juan Martínez of the Argentinian Central Bank said the bank uses reserve accumulation and carefully timed market participation to 'lean against the wind' and smooth peso fluctuations without a fixed rate.

On January 10, 2025, Canadian Minister of Innovation, Science and Industry Sophia LeBlanc launched an updated Foreign Investment Promotion and Protection Agreement (FIPA) to encourage foreign investment in technology and R&D while safeguarding national security and intellectual property.

Hedge fund manager David Goldberg said in a Bloomberg interview on February 23, 2025, that countries are more cautious about the international ramifications of their exchange rate policies, partly to avoid competitive devaluations and a 'race to the bottom'.
On March 4, 2025, UN Secretary-General António Guterres urged countries to align FDI policies with the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs).
IMF Chief Economist Gita Gopinath highlighted at the World Economic Forum in April 2025 how exchange rate stability can promote socially inclusive growth.
Smart contracts on blockchain platforms can automatically enforce foreign investment caps and repatriation limits.
The Chinese Central Bank adopted a new AI-based forecasting system on May 15, 2025, to fine-tune exchange rate policy.
The G20 summit in June 2025 showed renewed commitment to coordinating policy responses and avoiding competitive currency practices, with the WTO and IMF facilitating dialogue and frameworks.
